prs.title: Turbopack: ignore fully dynamic alternatives when tracing file paths
prs.author: mischnic
prs.body:
## Summary

With Turbopack, a file read whose path is _either_ an unknown value _or_ a known file traced the **entire project** into `.nft.json`, including `public/`. It also printed "Dynamic filesystem access causes tracing of the whole project". Two examples:

- `readFileSync(options.path ?? path.join(process.cwd(), 'manifest.json'))`
- a default parameter `p = path.join(process.cwd(), 'manifest.json')` that is then read

The default-parameter form regressed in 16.4: #97867 models default params as "caller's argument or the default". The `??` form behaved like this before.

A bare unknown path (`readFileSync(p)`) is already skipped when `ignore_dynamic_requests` is on, as it is for Next.js server and client code. The mixed case slipped through because `has_constant_parts()` is true as soon as _any_ alternative is constant. The unbounded alternative then resolved to every file in the project.

### Approach

A new `Pattern::filter_non_dynamic()` in `turbopack-core` keeps only the top-level alternatives that have constant parts. When dynamic requests are ignored, the file-tracing handlers trace that filtered pattern. The handlers are: fs reads, `fs.readdir`, `path.join`, `path.resolve`, `child_process.spawn` (its file reference) and `child_process.fork`. As a result:

- the known file is traced, and the unknown alternative is ignored, just as a bare unknown path is;
- fully dynamic patterns behave as before: a "very dynamic" lint, then skip;
- partially bounded paths such as `
…(truncated)

prs.title: turbo-persistence: parallelize large batch_get reads
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
### What?

Parallelize large `TurboPersistence::batch_get` calls in `turbo-persistence`.

- Batches with **more than 2048 keys** (`PARALLEL_BATCH_GET_THRESHOLD`) are split into chunks and run on the database's existing `ParallelScheduler`. Smaller batches run serially, one chunk per shard.
- `split_into_batch_chunks` aims for **4 chunks per task the scheduler can run at the same time** (like `turbo_tasks::util::good_chunk_size`). Every chunk stays inside _one shard_ of the family's current shard index, so small shards produce smaller chunks.
- New `ParallelScheduler` methods:
  - `parallelism()`: the number of tasks the scheduler can run at once. The turbo-tasks scheduler returns `turbo_tasks::parallel::available_parallelism()`, `SerialScheduler` returns 1.
  - `try_parallel_for_each_task_mut`: runs exactly one task per (already chunked) item.
- Less memory traffic in `batch_get`:
  - The sort is over compact `(u64 hash, u32 index)` cells.
  - Values are materialized as soon as an SST lookup finds them and written directly into the output `Vec`. There is no final loop to re-order the results.
  - Parallel chunks write disjoint indices concurrently through a small `ConcurrentSlice`.
  - Each chunk tracks the keys already found in newer SST files with a `turbo_bitset::Bitset` backed by a `SmallVec`, plus a counter. The bitset is preallocated for the chunk's positions (`Bitset::with_len`) and its `SmallVec` stores up to 256 positions inline, so typical chunks don't heap-allocate
…(truncated)

prs.title: Turbopack: wait for trace file changes after format errors
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

`turbo-trace-server` no longer re-reads a trace file every 500 ms after it was rejected with a format error. It prints the error once, prints `Waiting for the trace file to change...`, and reads the file again only once it changes (different size, modification or creation time, or on unix a different file at the path) or is removed.

### Why?

`TraceReader::try_read` returned `true` after printing `Trace file error: ...`, so `TraceReader::run` slept 500 ms and read the whole file again, forever. With the `TRACEv1` header check (#99781), every old `TRACEv0` trace hit this: the server printed the same error twice a second (10 times in 5 s locally). Corrupt trace data behaved the same way.

### How?

- Both format-error paths (format detection, and decoding with `format.read`) take a metadata snapshot of the open file and poll the path's metadata once per second until it differs. Only metadata is compared, so a rewrite that keeps size and timestamps the same (and on unix the same file) isn't noticed.
- Valid traces, live tailing, I/O errors and `STOP_AT` behave as before.

### Verification

- New unit test: a `TRACEv0` file and a corrupt `TRACEv1` file are not read again for 2.5 s, and replacing them with a valid trace loads it. It failed before this change.
- New unit test for change detection: size change, same-size rewrite, replacement by another file, and removal.
- Manual, release `turbo-trace-server`:
  - `TRACEv0` file for 5 s: error printed once (before: 10 ti
…(truncated)

prs.title: Enforce strict rustdoc (incl. private items) across the Rust workspace
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

Makes rustdoc warnings fail CI for the whole Rust workspace, including private items, and fixes every existing warning so the new check starts green.

- New `scripts/check-rustdoc.sh` runs `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --workspace --no-deps --document-private-items`.
- The existing `rustdoc check` job in `build_and_test.yml` now runs that script before `scripts/deploy-turbopack-docs.sh`. The public `next-*` docs build is unchanged.
- Fixes the warnings across the workspace's Rust crates (turbo-tasks, turbo-tasks-backend, turbo-persistence, turbopack-*, next-core, next-api, next-napi-bindings, …).

### Why?

The existing `rustdoc check` job only documented the public items of five `next-*` crates and didn't treat warnings as errors. Broken intra-doc links and other rustdoc warnings went unnoticed everywhere else. Running strict private-items docs over the whole workspace found about 60 of them.

### How?

The Rust source changes are doc comments only. The only other doc edit is one link target in `singleton_pattern.md`. Nothing is silenced with `#[allow]`, and no imports or visibility changes were added for docs. Types of fix:

- **Unresolved links**: point to the correct full path (`turbo_tasks::…`, `crate::…`, `Self::…`). Some links named renamed or moved items, for example `Effect::apply` → `CapturedEffect::apply` and `dec_in_flight` → `decrement_in_flight`. Those now point to the current item.
- **Links to items rustdoc can't link to**: plain code text.

prs.title: turbo-persistence: use partition_point for batch lookup bounds
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
Follow-up to #100620, addressing [this review comment](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/100620#discussion_r4399047345).

### What?

`MetaFile::batch_lookup_entry` now finds the cells inside an SST file's hash range with `partition_point` instead of `binary_search_by`.

### Why?

The old code used `binary_search_by` with a comparator that never returns `Equal` (`.then(Ordering::Greater)` / `.then(Ordering::Less)`) and then took the insertion point with `.err().unwrap()`. `partition_point` states the bounds directly and is easier to read.

### How?

- Start: `cells.partition_point(|&(hash, _)| hash < range.min_hash)`, the first cell with `hash >= min_hash`.
- End: `cells.partition_point(|&(hash, _)| hash <= range.max_hash)`, the first cell with `hash > max_hash`.

Both return the same indices as before for every input, including duplicate hashes, empty slices, and bounds at `0` or `u64::MAX`. The now unused `Ordering` import is removed. There is no behavior change.

prs.title: Ignore expected upgrade nudges in Agent Feedback
prs.author: aurorascharff
prs.body:
### What?

- Exclude intentional one-time `SecurityFatalError` and `UpgradeNudgeError` upgrade stops from the private Agent Feedback reporting protocol.
- Keep retries that remain blocked, or documented remediation that fails, eligible as unexpected behavior.
- Add an Agent Feedback eval with one genuine documentation mismatch and one expected upgrade stop. It requires the documentation report and rejects any report for the expected stop.
- Add focused coverage for the internal protocol loader.

### Why?

The Next.js upgrade gate intentionally stops a successful command once, explains that an upgrade is recommended, and allows the next run to continue. Agents were treating that expected stop as a Next.js error and filing duplicate feedback. The private reporting protocol should distinguish the expected gate from an actual failure of the retry or remediation path.

This does not change the public generated `AGENTS.md` instructions.

### Verification

| Check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Agent Feedback CLI and protocol tests | 25 passed |
| Eval fixture/config validation | Passed |
| Prettier | Passed |
| Agent eval model run | Attempted twice with the rebuilt local package; both shared AI Gateway requests failed before model execution |

prs.title: Add experimental.hydrationChangeEvent flag
prs.author: acdlite
prs.body:
Adds an experimental config flag, `experimental.hydrationChangeEvent`, that opts the `app` directory into React's experimental release channel (`react@experimental`) — the same channel already selected by `taint`, `transitionIndicator`, `gestureTransition`, and `blockingSSR`.

The experimental React build ships React's internal `enableHydrationChangeEvent` feature flag, which isn't in React's canary channel yet. This flag lets teams try it ahead of that. It has no effect of its own beyond selecting the experimental React build.

The flag is wired through `needsExperimentalReact` on the Next.js side and the matching `use_react_experimental` switch in Turbopack, so both bundlers pick the experimental build.

Automated approvals will only run for members of the Vercel GitHub org who are also on an allowlist of core Next.js contributors.

I asked an agent to analyze the codebase and split it into areas with different owners. Each area can have its own review criteria. The initial set of areas and owners is just a starting point. Please submit changes, I know some of them will be wrong! The area-specific review criteria are also mostly empty.

I seeded the agent with a starting set of "core" criteria. These are also not set in stone. I collected them from our existing skills and my own institutional knowledge of our team's practices. Please submit changes if you disagree with any, or want to propose more.

prs.title: perf(turbopack): canonicalize async loader availability
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

Canonicalize async-loader availability before constructing loaders for dynamic `import()` and `next/dynamic`, so parents that make the same modules available share loader tasks instead of creating them once per page.

Lazy-compilation proxies keep their activation paths stable; their actual targets still use canonicalization when their closures contain no further lazy proxies.

### Why?

`AsyncLoaderModule` and `async_loader_chunk_item` are keyed by `AvailabilityInfo`. Both the available chunk groups and `entry_group` carry per-parent information. On v0 there are about 196K `async_loader_chunk_item` tasks for a few hundred targets.

Intersecting availability with reachable groups alone isn't enough: a module shared with every page, such as `react/jsx-runtime`, keeps that intersection different per page.

### How?

- **Precompute observed sets in `compute_chunk_group_info`.** Build a chunk-group graph from async, shared/shared-merged and collected references, then close over it per strongly connected component. For each async target, record the distinct chunk-group sets tested during chunking, their union, and whether it needs `entry_group`. Store this in a keyed cell on `ChunkGroupInfo`.
- **Canonical availability.** From the union, remove each observed set that misses the parent availability. The result answers every observed intersection question like the original and depends only on those answers, not the parent. It can include groups not originally available; i
…(truncated)

prs.title: perf(build): lazily require page-data helpers in build/utils
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

Defer the requires in `packages/next/src/build/utils.ts` that are only needed while collecting page data, so the main `next build` process no longer evaluates them at startup. The deferred modules are the edge sandbox, `load-components`, the incremental cache helper, app segment collection, the app/pages static-path builders and the HTTP agent setup.

### Why?

`build/utils` is loaded eagerly by the main process, through `build/index` and through route discovery → `get-page-static-info`. Its top-level imports pulled in large dependency graphs, including `compiled/edge-runtime`, the incremental cache / response cache, the tracer and OpenTelemetry. Those are only used by `isPageStatic` and the component-loading helpers, which run in the build workers. The main process paid for evaluating them before `build()` started, then never used them.

### How?

- Each of those dependencies is now `require`d at its call site, keeping the original call order. The types still come from `import type`.
- The side-effect imports at the top of the file (`require-hook`, `node-polyfill-crypto`, `node-environment`) are untouched, so initialization order is the same in the main process and in workers.
- After the change, the deferred modules are never loaded in the main process for the whole build. The work is removed, not moved inside `build()`.

prs.title: Show dev overlay errors before the indicator state is known
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
## Summary

In development, the dev overlay renders nothing until the HMR `sync` message arrives. That message tells the client whether the dev indicator is disabled, and the client waits for it so a disabled indicator doesn't briefly appear. The error overlay (redbox) sat behind the same check, though. If `sync` was delayed or lost, compile and runtime errors already reached the client state but no redbox was shown.

This PR keeps the indicator-readiness check only for the indicator UI, meaning the devtools indicator and its panels. The error overlay and the contexts it needs now render independently of it, so errors show as soon as they are known. When `sync` arrives normally, the indicator behaves the same as before.

#100628 removes the server-side cause of a delayed `sync` (waiting on the npm registry version check). This change is independent and protects the overlay from any other delay.

A regression test uses Playwright websocket routing to withhold only the `sync` message. For both the app and pages router, it checks that a module-not-found error still shows the redbox and that the devtools indicator stays hidden.

prs.title: Turbopack: fix trailing-slash package root resolution
prs.author: mischnic
prs.body:
### What?

Fix trailing-slash package-root resolution in Turbopack, including dynamic CommonJS requests with an empty runtime suffix.

### Why?

The package-root result could be keyed as a bare package request even when the request included a trailing slash. Dynamic module contexts then lacked the slash-root key and threw `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` for a valid package entry. Exact trailing-slash requests could also resolve the same folder twice through overlapping root and relative-subpath paths.

### How?

Resolve matching package roots once while preserving distinct bare and trailing-slash request keys. Only use relative-subpath resolution for patterns that can match deeper paths, leaving package-exports handling unchanged.

Add keyed Rust coverage for main/index fallback, exports and dynamic patterns, plus a loader-free execution fixture that distinguishes the package main from index and checks real and missing subpaths.

### Verification

- Confirmed the execution regression fails on the unfixed resolver and passes with the correction.
- `cargo nextest run -p turbopack-tests --test execution -E 'test(resolving)'` — 33 fixtures passed.
- `cargo test -p turbopack-core --lib` — 198 passed; 2 existing ignored benchmarks.

prs.author: timneutkens
prs.body:
`create-next-app` no longer asks "Would you like to use App Router? (recommended)". New projects always use the App Router.

**Why**

The App Router is the recommended default, and the interactive prompt only offered a way to pick the Pages Router by accident. A saved `app: false` preference from an earlier run also kept silently producing Pages Router projects.

**Approach**

- Remove the App Router toggle prompt and set `opts.app = true` unless `--no-app` or `--api` is passed.
- Drop `app` from the defaults/preferences display, so the "recommended defaults" and "reuse previous settings" summaries no longer list "App Router" / "Pages Router".
- Saved `app` preferences are ignored. `--no-app` remains as the explicit opt-out, so the existing Pages templates and their tests are unchanged.

**Validation**

- `prompts.test.ts`: removed the App Router prompt from the customize flow; the "reuse previous settings" test with a saved `app: false` now expects an `app/` directory.
- Type-checked `packages/create-next-app/index.ts` with no new errors. The create-next-app e2e tests were not run locally.

**Docs**

Removed the prompt line and "App Router" from the recommended defaults summary in the installation guide and the `create-next-app` CLI reference.

prs.title: Fix hangs and crashes for 204 responses from route handlers and deduped fetches
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
### What

`new Response(body, { status })` throws `Invalid response status code 204` for null body statuses (204, 205, 304) whenever `body` is non-null, and that includes an empty buffer. A few places buffer a response with `arrayBuffer()` and rebuild it, which turns a body-less response into an empty buffer:

- **Route handler prerender with `cacheComponents`** (`app-route/module.ts`). The throw happened inside a `.then` callback whose rejection nothing handled, so the prerender promise never settled. Any route handler returning 204, including the auto-implemented `OPTIONS` handler, hung until the function timeout, and a GET returning 204 hung `next build`. We hit this on nextjs.org: every `OPTIONS /feed.xml` logged an `unhandledRejection` and then a 60s `Vercel Runtime Timeout Error`.
- **Serving a cached app route response** (`build/templates/app-route.ts`), which rebuilt the response from the stored body and returned a 500. This runs on Vercel too, right after generation, so fixing only the prerender path would have turned the timeouts into 500s.
- **Fetches deduped through `workStore.pendingRevalidates`** (`patch-fetch.ts`). The origin response is buffered for any status, so when it was a 204, every waiting caller after the first threw.

### How

- On the in-memory paths (the route handler prerender and both `pendingRevalidates` producers), check `body === null` on the original response and skip `arrayBuffer()` entirely, so nothing is read or allocated. The route handler
